Azel
ā´zel
n. (a descendant of Saul through Jonathan, in the Benjamite genealogies; Hebrew Atsel)
Hebrew Atsel, from a root meaning to set aside, reserve, or lay up beside — a fitting name for a man whose whole significance is that a line was kept.

Biblical Definition

Azel is a man of Benjamin, descended from Saul through Jonathan by way of Mephibosheth, Micah, and their sons. He appears in the Chronicler's Benjamite genealogy and again, almost word for word, in the register of those who dwelt at Jerusalem after the captivity: “And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan” (1Ch 8:38). Nothing is told of him but his father, his six sons, and the fact that the same list was worth writing twice. That is the point of him. Saul's house had been struck down at Gilboa, hunted through the years of David's rise, and reduced at last to a lame child hidden at Lodebar. The dynasty was finished. Yet centuries later, when the exiles came home and the Chronicler set out to show that Israel still existed, the line of the rejected king was still there to be counted, six sons deep, living in Jerusalem. Azel is the evidence that God's rejection of a throne was not the extinction of a family.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) does not enter Azel; the name is fixed by the Hebrew text as a descendant of Saul.

expand to see more

The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.

AZEL. A Benjamite, descended from king Saul through Jonathan and Mephibosheth.

The Hebrew root signifies to set aside, to reserve, or to lay up beside.

His six sons are named identically in 1 Chronicles 8:38 and 1 Chronicles 9:44.

A place named Azal is mentioned in Zechariah 14:5, from a kindred form.

Key Scripture

1Ch 8:37 — "And Moza begat Binea: Rapha was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son:"

1Ch 8:38 — "And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel."

1Ch 9:43 — "And Moza begat Binea; and Rephaiah his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son."

1Ch 9:44 — "And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan: these were the sons of Azel."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's judgment on an office is not the annihilation of a household.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Azel is a name in a list twice repeated, and no one contests him. The temptation is simply to skip both lists.

The principle to recover is the difference between a judgment and an erasure. The LORD rejected Saul from being king, and the sentence was executed — the kingdom was rent from him and given to a neighbour better than he, and his sons fell with him in one day on Gilboa. But the sentence fell on the throne, not on the blood. David sought out whether any remained of the house of Saul that he might shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake, and set Mephibosheth at his own table continually. From that preserved cripple the line ran down through Micah and Moza to Azel and his six sons, and was still in Jerusalem after the exile, still worth a full entry. God is exact in His judgments and never wasteful with them. He removed a crown and kept a family, and He noted their names twice so that no one reading would think the house had simply vanished.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Atsel (H682), Azel; from atsal (H680), to set aside, reserve, lay up beside.

expand to see more

Hebrew Atsel (H682) — Azel, a Benjamite of Saul's house; 1 Chronicles 8:37-38, 9:43-44.

Hebrew atsal (H680) — to lay aside, reserve, keep back; Numbers 11:17.

Hebrew Merib-baal / Mephibosheth (H4648) — Jonathan's son, in this line; 2 Samuel 9:6.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — kindness; the ground of David's dealing with the house, 2 Samuel 9:1.

The genealogy is given twice, in the Benjamite list and among the dwellers at Jerusalem.

Usage

"“Azel had six sons” — the same six names recorded twice over."

"“All these were the sons of Azel” — a rejected house still counted."

"“Eleasah his son, Azel his son” — Saul's line traced past the exile."
